title: Perfect competition

definition.text: An idealized market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price.

facts.text: Under its conditions a market reaches an equilibrium where supply equals demand for every product, including labour, and this equilibrium is Pareto optimal.
Every profit-maximizing firm ends up charging a price equal to its marginal cost, which makes the market allocatively efficient.
Without externalities and public goods, such equilibria are Pareto-efficient: a result called the First Theorem of Welfare Economics.
Each firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve, so it must take the market price.
In the long run no firm earns economic profit, because any profit draws in new firms until the price falls to average cost.
Real markets come close to it mainly for farm products and raw materials sold by many sellers to many buyers.
Critics say it treats firms as passive, ignoring price-cutting, product design, advertising and innovation, and leaves unclear who actually sets prices.

contested_note: Critics dispute the realism of its assumptions and whether a model of price-takers can describe a decentralized market at all.

definition.text: The return that just makes running a business worthwhile, equal to what the owner's time and capital could earn in their next best use.

facts.text: Economists count normal profit as a cost, not as part of business profit.
It varies within and across industries in line with how risky each kind of investment is.
Under perfect competition only normal profits survive in the long run, so firms have no reason to enter or leave the industry.
Profits above normal persist only where barriers to entry stop new firms from coming in, as in monopoly or oligopoly.

definition.text: The price below which a loss-making firm does better to stop producing in the short run: the point where price falls under average variable cost.

facts.text: Shutting down avoids variable costs but not fixed costs, which must be paid anyway and so are ignored in the decision.
A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve at and above the shutdown point.

definition.text: The amount of money buyers are willing and able to pay for a good or service and that sellers are willing to accept.

facts.text: Prices are shaped by production costs, by supply and by demand, and may be set by a monopolist or imposed by market conditions.
Price theory says that in a free market the price settles where the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded.
Milton Friedman named five functions of prices, including passing on information, giving incentives to produce what is valued, and rationing fixed supplies among consumers.
Price is what the buyer pays; cost of production is the seller's own spending on making the product, and the two are different things.
Adam Smith's diamond–water paradox asks why diamonds cost more than water, though water is essential to life and diamonds are mere ornament.
Carl Menger's theory of marginal utility was offered as one answer to that paradox.
In April 2020 the price of West Texas Intermediate crude for May delivery turned negative for the first time, at -$37.63 a barrel.

definition.text: A price below zero, where the owner or producer pays the 'buyer' to take an item away.

facts.text: In April 2020 oil for May delivery fell to -$37.63 a barrel, a one-day drop of $55.90, because holders feared there was nowhere left to store it.
Negative interest rates are a similar idea.
